**Before this page:** [interval arithmetic](interval-arithmetic.qmd),
[zonotopes](zonotopes.qmd), [intervals and zonotopes
together](intervals-and-zonotopes.qmd) and [certified funnels and
composition](funnel-composition.qmd). Each section below follows the same
pattern: the problem, a tiny example, the fix, why the fix is sound, and
where it showed up.

## 1. Index the tube by progress, not by time

**Problem.** A tube indexed by *time* asks where every state is at time
$t$. In an unstable phase, such as a box tipping over a corner, small
differences in timing grow, so at a fixed time the set spreads over a wide
range of tilts, and every condition must hold over that whole range.

**Tiny example.** Let the tilt grow as $\theta(t)=\theta_0e^{1.2t}$ with
$\theta_0\in[0.08,0.12]$. At $t=1.6$ the set spans tilts $0.55$ to $0.82$,
and it keeps widening. At the tilt $0.5$, the same motions differ only in
*when* they arrive (times $1.19$ to $1.53$), and their state there is the
same tilt.

![Time-indexed versus progress-indexed tubes on a diverging tipping motion. Left: at a fixed time the set spans a wide range of tilts. Right: at a fixed tilt (one band) the spread is only in arrival time. Drawn by `scripts/bg_certification_figures.py`.](media/bg_band_vs_time.svg){.lightbox}

**Fix.** Index the tube by a progress variable that the motion advances
monotonically (the tilt, or the box's position on a transport), cut it into
**bands**, and certify that each step carries every state of a band into a
later band. Timing drops out; only the *transverse* deviation (rate error,
contact places) is carried.

**Why it is sound.** The certificate also proves that progress per step is
at least one band, so every state leaves each band forward, and the bands
cover the whole range without gaps.

**In our chain.** A zonotope tube for the push, indexed by time, was
refused at step 14: the set spread in progress along the divergent tipping
and the mean-value remainder blew up. The band tube for the same push holds
(utilization 0.484).

## 2. Split the entry set, keep one law

**Problem.** A certificate over a large entry set can fail because a single
box is too coarse (see [bisection](interval-arithmetic.qmd)), not because
the law is wrong.

**Tiny example.** On $[0.5,1]^2$ the interval lower bound of $x\cdot y$ is
$0.25$; on the right half $[0.75,1]\times[0.5,1]$ it is $0.375$. The same
property, split, certifies where it holds.

![Bisection: one box, then 4, then 16 pieces; the number in each is the interval lower bound of x·y, against the requirement 0.3. Drawn by `scripts/bg_certification_figures.py`.](media/bg_bisection.svg){.lightbox}

**Fix.** Split the entry set into sub-boxes and certify each one, **with the
same law on every piece**. The union of the certified pieces is a certified
entry set for that law.

**Why it is sound.** Each sub-box's certificate holds for every state in it;
the union of the sub-boxes covers the entry set; one law means the executed
controller does not depend on which piece the state is in.

**In our chain.**

- The push after the roll: a single tube over the roll's whole certified
  exit set is refused at every push magnitude (progress per step falls
  below one band); on a $2\times8$ partition, 16 of 16 sub-boxes certify
  with one push of 0.1116 N (utilization 0.686).
- The floor-corner lift's departure: over its whole start box the
  departure condition's margin is $-0.085$ (refused), and on $8\times8$
  pieces every piece certifies. The whole-box margin is itself the result
  of keeping a correlation: carrying the step-corner place as a function of
  the box pose (a mean-value form on the pose generators, remainder 0.5 µm)
  narrows it from $[60.484,61.005]$ mm to $[60.615,60.873]$ mm and raises the
  whole-box margin from $-0.470$ to $-0.085$ ([same hull, different
  set](zonotopes.qmd)).

## 3. Choose the pivot in interval elimination

**Problem.** Solving a linear system whose coefficients are intervals by
Gaussian elimination divides by the pivots. If a pivot's interval contains
or nearly contains zero, the quotient blows up, and every later quantity
inherits the blow-up.

**Tiny example.** Solve $\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}x=b$
with $\varepsilon\in[-0.01,0.01]$. Pivoting on $\varepsilon$ divides by an
interval containing $0$: no bound at all. Swapping the rows and pivoting on
$1$ gives the next pivot $1-\varepsilon\in[0.99,1.01]$: perfectly
tame.

**Fix.** Order the rows by pivoting on the coefficients' **midpoints**; fix
that order for the evaluation; and still check that every pivot's interval
excludes zero.

**Why it is sound.** Any row order gives the same solution set; the
interval elimination is sound for whichever order is used, provided no
pivot interval contains zero, and that is checked.

**In our chain.** In the landing's impact window, the make class with both
the step corner and the platform's far support sticking used a fixed order
whose first pivot was near zero. Pivoting on the midpoints cut the census
of the cover from $1.7\times10^7$ to $4.7\times10^4$ pieces. Two soundness
audits checked certified cells against sampled trajectories and exact
arithmetic: on the earlier landing set, 1000 cells, 906,497 step checks
and 176,540 exact rational solves of that system; on the current landing
set's preview roots, 463 cells, 221,192 step checks and 76,830 exact
solves. In all, 1,127,689 step checks (0 states outside the propagated
zonotopes, 0 excluded classes taken) and 253,370 exact solves (0 outside
the enclosure, 0 pivot enclosures containing zero).

## 4. A kink inside one formation: the support-switch band

**Problem.** Inside a single contact formation the force model can change:
on the platform transport, the flush contact's left support moves from the
step corner to the box's own corner as the box slides past half its width.
The margins are smooth on either side but have a kink at the switch, and a
band that straddles the switch cannot use either model alone.

**Tiny example.** Model A's margin is $0.30-0.25x$, model B's is
$0.1625+0.30(x-0.55)$, and the true margin follows A before $x=0.55$ and B
after it. On a band $[0.43,0.67]$ across the switch, the bound
$\min(A,B)$ is valid wherever the state actually is.

![A support switch inside one formation: two force models and the band's bound, the minimum over both. Schematic. Drawn by `scripts/bg_certification_figures.py`.](media/bg_switch_band.svg){.lightbox}

**Fix.** Near the switch, the band's step image is the **hull of both
models' enclosures**, each condition's bound is the **minimum over both**,
and the two support conditions only define which piece each state is on. A
term that is implied by a piece's own support condition may be dropped only
on that model's piece.

**Why it is sound.** At every state in the band the true dynamics is one of
the two models, so the true next state lies in one of the two enclosures
(hence in their hull) and every true margin is at least the smaller bound.

**In our chain.** With the switch band, the goal transport ends at a section
past the switch, where the rest at the goal certifies with both supports on
the box's corners, instead of a 32 µm window before it.

## 5. One contact definition, three readers

**Problem.** The recognizer (which contacts are on), the certifier's
reduction (which constraints a formation imposes) and the planner's gate
must agree on what a contact *is*. If one reader sees a contact that is not
there, the others certify the wrong thing.

**Tiny example.** Two edges that are parallel and within the tolerance of
each other, but meet only at a single point that another closed contact
already holds, look "flush" to a distance test. Under Xiao and Ji's rule a
contact counts only if it is not contained in a larger one, so that pair is
not a separate contact.

**Fix.** Apply Xiao–Ji containment on the actual contact region, with no
new constant, in all three readers. The certifier's version must be a
**sound sufficient** form of the recognizer's: whenever the certifier says
"contained (open)", the recognizer must too; the two are cross-tested.

**Why it is sound.** A sufficient form can only refuse more, never certify
a contact reading the recognizer would not produce.

**In our chain.** The recognizer read the box's bottom face flush with the
riser for box positions $x_B\in[61.5,63.5]$ mm, although the two edges
meet only at the step corner, already in the platform contact. That phantom
contact stopped a certified transport short of the lift goal. Under the
containment rule (issue #53) it is gone, and the 200 held-out and 34 test
searches are re-run under it.

## 6. Keep the speed continuous at a junction

**Problem.** If one funnel ends at one speed and the next funnel's law
demands a much higher speed at once, the step after the junction needs a
large acceleration, and the forces that produce it can leave their friction
cones.

**Tiny example.** Raising a tilt rate from 1°/s to 8°/s within one
$10$ ms step is an angular acceleration of about $12$ rad/s², far more than
the slow, held motion before the junction ever needed.

**Fix.** Keep the incoming speed: certify the next funnel with a law that
starts at the previous funnel's speed, from the previous funnel's
**certified** exit.

**Why it is sound.** The junction is then an ordinary certified containment
([composition](funnel-composition.qmd)): the next funnel is verified with
its entry equal to the previous certified exit.

**In our chain.** The floor-corner lift ends at 1°/s. The roll at 8°/s could
not be certified from the lift's exit: the junction failed on the step
corner's friction cone and on the exclusion of other contact classes. The
roll at 1°/s, verified from the lift's certified exit, holds (utilization
0.2435), and its own certificate to the 88.16° hand-off holds at 0.376 with
765 of 765 held-out rollouts inside.

## What to remember

- **Index tubes by progress**, not time, wherever the motion is unstable.
- **Split the entry set, keep one law**; the union of certified pieces is
  certified.
- **Pivot on midpoints** and check every pivot excludes zero; the order
  changes the bound, not the soundness.
- **At a kink inside a formation**, take the hull of both models and the
  minimum of both bounds.
- **One contact definition** for every reader; the certifier's form is a
  sound sufficient version of the recognizer's.
- **Keep speeds continuous at junctions**, and compose from certified exits.
